messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Fatima's Burden

Fatima had spent forty-two years on the bench, a reputation built on careful deliberation and measured judgment. At seventy-five, she had presided over hundreds of cases, her chambers a place where people came expecting clarity and fairness. Her colleagues respected her; her family—her husband Karim of fifty-three years, her three adult children, her seven grandchildren—had learned long ago that she brought the same precision to family decisions that she brought to the law. She was the one people called when there was a problem to solve, a conflict to untangle, a choice to be made. This was who Fatima had always been: steady, capable, in control.

Six months ago, her youngest daughter Layla, thirty-eight years old, had collapsed at work without warning. A ruptured aneurysm, the doctors said—something no one could have predicted, no scan that would have caught it beforehand. Fatima had been in her chambers when the call came. She remembered the particular quality of the silence in the room afterward, the way her hand had continued to hold the phone even after the line went dead. Layla died in the hospital three hours later, with Karim at her bedside and Fatima still driving, still in that suspended state between knowing and not knowing.

In the weeks that followed, Fatima found herself returning obsessively to the days before Layla's death. She had spoken to her daughter on the phone the evening before the collapse—a brief, ordinary conversation about Layla's son's soccer schedule. Fatima had been distracted, reviewing a brief for a case. She had cut the call short. Now she was certain that if she had paid closer attention, if she had asked the right questions, if she had pressed Layla about how she was feeling, she might have noticed something amiss. Some mothers would have. A better mother would have heard the subtle signs of illness in her daughter's voice. Fatima had not. She had hung up and returned to her work.

The self-recrimination had calcified into something harder over the months. She had come to believe that her reactions since Layla's death proved what she had always suspected about herself underneath the professional veneer: she was a poor coper, a woman whose composure masked a fundamental inadequacy. Real mothers, she thought, would have protected their children. Real mothers would have found a way. She should have been more present, more vigilant, more something. The fact that she had not—the fact that she had failed at the one role that mattered most—seemed to her irrefutable evidence of a character flaw so deep that no amount of judicial wisdom could compensate for it. On the bench, she could control outcomes through careful reasoning. In life, where it counted, she had proven useless.

Work had become increasingly difficult. Cases that once engaged her now felt hollow. She would sit through arguments and find her mind elsewhere, or worse, find herself imagining worst-case scenarios for the families involved in the litigation before her. She had taken a leave of absence three months ago, telling the court she needed time to grieve. What she could not say was that she no longer trusted her own judgment—not about law, not about anything. If she had failed to protect her own daughter, what business did she have deciding the fates of other people's families?

Karim had suggested she speak to someone. He said it gently, the way he said most things now, carefully avoiding any suggestion that she was not coping well, though they both knew that was precisely what he meant. Fatima had resisted. What could a therapist tell her that she did not already know? That she should forgive herself? That Layla's death was not her fault? These were comforting platitudes, and Fatima had never been one for comfort that was not earned. But last week, sitting alone in her study at three in the morning—unable to sleep, unable to stop thinking about all the ways she had failed—she had finally called. She was not here because she believed she could be fixed. She was here because she had nowhere else to go, and because the weight of her own judgment of herself had become unbearable.
